That this formulation has stood the test of time in obvious from the fact that as late as in 1950 in explaining the doctrine, Lord Porter in his Speech before the House of Lords in the case of Barkway Vs. Southwales Transport (1950) 1 A.E.R. 392, recited with approval the above-quoted observation of Chief Justice Erle. From the above formulation it is clear that the said maxim is a kind of rule of presumption in the absence of evidence relating to the particulars of the accident and can therefore have no application, when all relevant facts have been proved or are known. 

 26. No reasonable explanation on behalf of the defendants as to the cause of the fall of the C.I. sheet is forthcoming. Under the circumstances, the Court is inevitably led to the presumption that there was want of due and proper care on the part of defendant No. 2.
